title: LEADERSHIP: In the Face of Adversity, Leaders Must Redefine Success
author: Admired Leadership
summary: When adversity disrupts an organisation's original mission, lowering the bar or setting new targets is insufficient. Leaders must understand the psychological distinction between goals (measurable targets) and success (a narrative that answers whether the work still matters). Team members need more than a revised scorecard; they need a compelling story about why their effort is still worthy. Leaders must first acknowledge the setback honestly -- admitting disappointment, describing the cause -- before pivoting to a new direction. Simple reframing ('focus on the learning,' 'use this as a reset') reads as spin that teams immediately detect. The new success definition should focus on what the team controls and why it matters, proving character and adaptability regardless of outcome. Teams that receive both new goals and a new success narrative consistently emerge from adversity stronger, carrying confidence that favorable circumstances alone cannot manufacture.
points: Goals are measurable targets; success is a narrative answering the existential team question: does what I am doing still matter?
Simple reframing ('focus on the learning') is detectable as spin -- teams want a compelling new challenge, not a consolation prize.
Leaders must acknowledge the setback honestly and admit disappointment before redefining success; skipping this undermines credibility.
The new success definition must be within the team's control and prove character -- not depend on favorable circumstances.
Teams given both new goals and a new success narrative consistently outperform those given only revised targets.
quotes: Goals are measurable targets. Success, by contrast, is a narrative. It answers the question that every team member is quietly asking: Does what I'm doing still matter?
Good leaders don't redefine success by packaging disappointment as opportunity. Teams can quickly sniff out the 'spin' of simple reframing.
Before crafting a new narrative of success, leaders must first acknowledge the setback and the reason for a shift to a new direction. They must get honest and admit their disappointment.
Success is now defined by what the team must do to prove itself, regardless of the outcome that adversity has taken off the table.

Teams with new goals and a new redefinition of success commonly emerge stronger from adversity. And when the headwinds finally ease, they carry with them the hard-won confidence and attitude that no perfect set of circumstances can manufacture on its own.
